I'm not certain what you are referring to. I can say it is unlikely that I would harvest honey. My wife is vegan and it is a no honey household. I just thought it might be interesting and educational for my children.

OK. This give is generating alot of interest in beekeeping, but there isn't a shortcut around managing the colony and learning the art of beekeeping.

I suggest that you'd do much better getting a traditional hive and setting up an observation hive for your kids the second season when you're more comfortable.

It's a rewarding experience for much more than the honey and is an art as much as it is a science.

I can only assume you want to keep bees for the environmental impact, yes? If so, put more effort into solitary bees and not honey bees. Honey bees are an import from Europe and not native to the USA. A carpenter bee is a 20X more efficient pollinator and can pollinate an entire apple tree in a day. There are many tutorials online to provide homes for carpenter bees.

He's talking about the Flow Hive, I'm guessing. I highly recommend getting into beekeeping (suburban beekeeper here). It's incredibly rewarding, fun, and it just feels great watching those bees rush in and out of the hive all day. You don't have to harvest honey if you want but you'll be able to sell it for a nice price to friends and family at the least. You can also harvest beeswax of which you can make cosmetics and candles. You can also sell the beeswax of course in bulk. For me beekeeping relaxes me, my neighbors appreciate the free pollination of their fruit trees (bigger fruit more fruit per tree), plus I enjoy the added income of the honey and wax. The downside is that it can be quite expensive to get started (~$300 for hive and equipment plus ~$150-200 for bees for one hive) plus you can't really take any honey or wax for the first year. I would highly recommend getting two hives to start if you are going to start as you can compare the two to learn quicker plus you have one left over if one dies out. I also recommend reading up on it substantially before starting. Get in touch with a local beekeeper and just ask them about your area as far as when the nectar flows are or how difficult it is to keep a hive there. It really isn't that difficult but knowing more about it will give you a leg up and help you avoid potential issues before they arise. I would definitely suggest reconsidering the "no honey household" as the bees make far more (usually) than they can make use of (think of taking honey like charging rent) plus it's really good for those that suffer seasonal allergies. If you have any questions feel free to shoot me a message and I will help you as best as I can or at least point you in the right direction! Best of luck with your bees if you decide to get them!
